title: Part II: Bhakti-Sufi Traditions: Changes in Religious Beliefs and Devotional Texts

topics.title: A mosaic of beliefs: the integration of cults

learn.hook: At Puri, a wooden image carved by local tribal specialists came to be worshipped as Jagannatha, a form of Vishnu. How do local gods join a larger tradition?
points: From about the eighth century, sculpture and texts show a striking variety of gods and goddesses, such as Vishnu, Shiva and many forms of the goddess, worshipped across the subcontinent.

Historians see at least two processes at work. One was the spread of Brahmanical ideas through the composition, compilation and preservation of Puranic texts in simple Sanskrit verse, accessible to women and Shudras. The other was that Brahmanas accepted and reworked the beliefs and practices of other social groups.

At Puri (Odisha), by the twelfth century, a local deity, whose image was and still is made of wood by local tribal specialists, came to be identified as a form of Vishnu: Jagannatha, literally 'lord of the world'.

Local goddesses, often worshipped as a stone smeared with ochre, were incorporated into the Puranic framework by being identified as wives of the principal male deities: sometimes Lakshmi, wife of Vishnu, and sometimes Parvati, wife of Shiva.

The sociologist Robert Redfield described the practices of dominant groups such as priests and rulers as the 'great' tradition and those of peasants and others as 'little' traditions. He noted that both changed through their interaction.

example.q: How do historians explain the integration of a local deity like Jagannatha into a wider tradition?
steps: A local deity had its own worshippers and tribal specialists.
Brahmanas identified it with Vishnu, a Puranic god.
Its worship then became part of a wider Vaishnava tradition, while keeping local features.
This illustrates interaction between 'great' and 'little' traditions.
example.answer: By showing how a local deity was identified with a Puranic god, which blended local and Brahmanical traditions.

learn.reallife: The annual Rath Yatra of Lord Jagannatha at Puri draws lakhs of devotees, and the wooden images are still renewed in the Nabakalebara ceremony.

topics.title: Tantra, conflict and two kinds of bhakti

learn.hook: Some worshipped a god with a face, ornaments and stories; others worshipped a god beyond all form. Both paths are called bhakti!
points: Tantric practices were widespread in several parts of the subcontinent. They were open to women and men, and practitioners often ignored differences of caste and class within the ritual context.
Many Tantric ideas influenced Shaivism and Buddhism, especially in the eastern, northern and southern parts of the subcontinent. Tantric practitioners often ignored the authority of the Vedas.

There were often tensions: those who valued the Vedic tradition condemned practices outside regulated sacrifice; devotees often projected their chosen deity, Vishnu or Shiva, as supreme. Relations with Buddhism and Jainism were also often tense, if not marked by open conflict.

Bhakti traditions are classified into two broad categories. Saguna bhakti ('with attributes') focuses on specific deities such as Shiva, Vishnu and his avatars, and forms of the goddess, often in human form. Nirguna bhakti ('without attributes') is the worship of an abstract form of god.

Timeline of religious teachers: Appar and Sambandar (Tamil Nadu, c. 6th–8th centuries) → Andal and Nammalvar (Tamil Nadu, c. 8th–9th) → Basavanna (Karnataka, 12th) → Nizamuddin Auliya (Delhi, 14th) → Kabir, Guru Nanak (15th–16th) → Mirabai (16th).

example.q: Classify: (a) worship of Krishna as a beloved with a flute; (b) devotion to a formless Ultimate Reality.
steps: Krishna has a form, stories and attributes.
So (a) is saguna bhakti.
A formless reality has no attributes.
So (b) is nirguna bhakti.

learn.reallife: Bhajans to Krishna sung at ISKCON temples (saguna) and the Gurbani hymns sung in gurdwaras to the formless Waheguru (nirguna) show both bhakti forms alive today.

topics.title: The Alvars and Nayanars: poems of prayer

learn.hook: Some Tamil saints claimed their hymns were as important as the Vedas. They came from all walks of life, including castes considered 'untouchable'!
points: Some of the earliest bhakti movements (c. sixth century) were led by the Alvars ('those who are immersed in devotion to Vishnu') and the Nayanars ('leaders who were devotees of Shiva') in Tamil Nadu.

They travelled from place to place singing hymns in Tamil in praise of their gods. They identified certain shrines as abodes of their chosen deities; large temples were later built at many of these sites, which became pilgrimage centres. Singing their compositions became part of temple rituals.

By the tenth century, the compositions of the 12 Alvars were compiled in an anthology, the Nalayira Divyaprabandham ('Four Thousand Sacred Compositions'), often described as the Tamil Veda. The Nayanars' hymns were compiled as the Tevaram.

Some historians suggest these saints protested against, or tried to reform, the caste system and Brahmana dominance, since bhaktas came from diverse backgrounds: Brahmanas, artisans, cultivators and even castes considered 'untouchable'. Their claim that their compositions were as important as the Vedas also points to this.

Women devotees were important. Andal, a woman Alvar, saw herself as the beloved of Vishnu; her compositions are still widely sung. Karaikkal Ammaiyar, a devotee of Shiva, adopted extreme asceticism. These women renounced their social obligations but did not join an alternative order or become nuns, challenging patriarchal norms.

example.q: How did the Alvars and Nayanars express criticism of the caste system?
steps: They came from many castes, including those considered 'untouchable'.
They welcomed devotees regardless of birth.
They claimed their Tamil hymns were as important as the Sanskrit Vedas.
This challenged Brahmana dominance over sacred knowledge.
example.answer: Through their diverse backgrounds, their open devotion and their claim that Tamil hymns equalled the Vedas.

learn.reallife: Andal's Tiruppavai is recited every year in the Tamil month of Margazhi (December–January) in homes and temples across Tamil Nadu.

topics.title: Bhakti saints and the state in the Tamil region

learn.hook: The Cholas built gigantic temples like the Brihadeshwara at Thanjavur and even had bronze images of Nayanar saints made. Royal power and devotion went hand in hand!
points: Between the sixth and ninth centuries, the Tamil region had powerful chiefdoms such as the Pallavas and Pandyas. Buddhism and Jainism had been prevalent for centuries, drawing support from merchant and artisan communities.
A major theme in Tamil bhakti hymns is the poets' opposition to Buddhism and Jainism, especially in the Nayanars' compositions. Historians attribute this hostility to competition for royal patronage.
The powerful Chola rulers (ninth to thirteenth centuries) supported Brahmanical and bhakti traditions, making land grants and building temples for Vishnu and Shiva.
The magnificent Shiva temples at Chidambaram, Thanjavur and Gangaikondacholapuram were built under Chola patronage. This period also saw some of the most spectacular bronze sculptures of Shiva.

Chola rulers introduced the singing of Tamil Shaiva hymns in temples under royal patronage and took the initiative to collect and organise them into a text. They used the saints' popularity to claim divine support and legitimise their power; for example, metal images of Nayanar saints were consecrated in Shiva temples.

example.q: Why did Chola kings support bhakti saints and temples?
steps: Bhakti saints were very popular among the people.
Supporting their traditions and building temples showed the king as a devotee.
This helped kings claim divine support for their rule.
So patronage strengthened royal legitimacy.
example.answer: Supporting bhakti and temples linked the kings to popular devotion and divine support, strengthening their power.

learn.reallife: The Brihadeshwara temple at Thanjavur, part of the UNESCO 'Great Living Chola Temples', celebrated its 1,000th year in 2010.

learn.hook: In twelfth-century Karnataka, a movement taught that every devotee, whatever their caste, could reach Shiva. Its followers wear a small linga on their body to this day!
points: In the twelfth century, a new movement emerged in Karnataka, led by Basavanna (1106–68), a Brahmana who was initially a Jaina and a minister at a royal court in Karnataka.

His followers were known as Virashaivas (heroes of Shiva) or Lingayats (wearers of the linga). They worship Shiva in the form of a linga, and men usually wear a small linga in a silver case on a loop strung over the left shoulder. Wandering monks called jangama are revered.

Lingayats believe that on death the devotee will be united with Shiva and will not return to this world. Therefore they do not practise funerary rites such as cremation, but ceremonially bury their dead.

They challenged the idea of caste and the 'pollution' attributed to certain groups by Brahmanas, and questioned the theory of rebirth. They won followers among those who were marginalised within the Brahmanical social order. They also encouraged practices disapproved in the Dharmashastras, such as post-puberty marriage and the remarriage of widows.
Our knowledge of the tradition comes from vachanas (literally 'sayings'), composed in Kannada by women and men who joined the movement.

example.q: Why did the Virashaivas challenge the caste system?
steps: They believed all devotees could unite with Shiva.
They rejected the idea that some groups were 'polluting'.
They questioned rebirth, which justified caste by past actions.
So caste had no basis in their belief, and they drew followers from marginalised groups.
example.answer: Because they believed in devotion to Shiva open to all, rejected pollution and rebirth, and so rejected birth-based hierarchy.

learn.reallife: Basava Jayanti is celebrated across Karnataka, and Basavanna's vachanas are part of Kannada school and college syllabuses.

topics.title: North India's religious ferment and the faiths of rulers and subjects

learn.hook: Naths and Jogis questioned rituals with simple logic, while Arab merchants settled on the Malabar coast. New ideas were arriving from many directions!
points: In north India, the same period saw the emergence of several Rajput states. In most of them, Brahmanas held positions of importance, performing a range of secular and ritual functions.

Religious leaders outside the orthodox Brahmanical framework gained ground: the Naths, Jogis and Siddhas. Many came from artisanal groups, including weavers. They criticised rituals and the social order using simple, logical arguments, advocated renunciation and meditation on the formless ultimate reality, and used yogasanas, breathing exercises and meditation. They were popular among 'low' castes and paved the way for devotional religion.
The arrival of the Turks culminated in the establishment of the Delhi Sultanate in the thirteenth century. This undermined the power of many Rajput states and the Brahmanas associated with them.

Islam had arrived earlier: Arab merchants frequented ports along the western coast, and Arab armies conquered Sind in 711, making it part of the Caliph's domain. Later Turks, Afghans and then the Mughals set up states. In theory, Muslim rulers were to be guided by the ulama and to rule according to the sharia.

Many subjects were not Muslims. The category of zimmi (protected people, from the Arabic zimma, protection) applied to people with revealed scriptures, such as Jews and Christians, who paid a tax called jizya in return for protection. In India this status was extended to Hindus. Rulers often followed flexible policies: several, including Mughals, gave land endowments and tax exemptions to Hindu, Jaina, Zoroastrian, Christian and Jewish institutions.

example.q: Why did many Muslim rulers adopt flexible policies towards their subjects?
steps: Most subjects were not Muslims.
Rulers needed their support and revenue.
The zimmi category offered protection in return for jizya.
Many rulers also gave grants to non-Muslim institutions to win goodwill.
example.answer: Because they ruled over largely non-Muslim populations and needed their cooperation, they offered protection and patronage.

learn.reallife: Gorakhnath, a famous figure of the Nath tradition, gives his name to Gorakhpur in Uttar Pradesh, home to the Gorakhnath temple.

topics.title: Islam in practice: pillars, sects and local adaptations

learn.hook: A mosque in Kerala with a sloping, temple-like roof, and Khojah devotional songs in Gujarati sung in ragas: Islam took many local forms in India.
points: All those who adopted Islam accepted, in principle, the five 'pillars' of the faith: that there is one God, Allah, and Prophet Muhammad is his messenger (shahada); offering prayers five times a day (namaz/salat); giving alms (zakat); fasting during the month of Ramzan (sawm); and performing the pilgrimage to Mecca (hajj).
This universal faith was often coloured by sectarian affiliations, Sunni and Shi'a, by schools of law such as the Hanafi and Shafi'i, and by local customs of converts.

The Khojahs, a branch of the Ismailis (a Shi'a sect), spread ideas from the Qur'an through indigenous literary forms. The ginan (from the Sanskrit jnana, 'knowledge') were devotional poems in Punjabi, Multani, Sindhi, Kachchi, Hindi and Gujarati, sung in special ragas during daily prayer.

Arab Muslim traders who settled on the Malabar coast (Kerala) married local women; they came to be known as Mappilas. They learnt Malayalam and adopted local customs such as matriliny and matrilocality. Mosque architecture combined universal elements, like orientation towards Mecca, with local features: sloping roofs in Kerala, brick in Bengal, and wooden architecture in Kashmir.

Sanskrit texts and inscriptions of the eighth to fourteenth centuries rarely used the term 'Muslim'. People were classified by place of origin: Turushka (Turks), Tajika (people from Tajikistan), Parashika (people from Persia). The term mlechchha was used for migrants who did not observe caste norms and spoke non-Sanskritic languages; it was sometimes derogatory but did not denote a religious identity.

example.q: Why do historians say Islam in India was not a single uniform practice?
steps: The five pillars were shared by all.
But there were sects (Sunni, Shi'a) and schools of law.
Local communities like Khojahs and Mappilas adapted to local languages and customs.
Mosque styles varied by region.
example.answer: Because shared beliefs combined with sectarian differences and local adaptations in language, custom and architecture.

learn.reallife: The Cheraman Juma Masjid at Kodungallur in Kerala, often described as one of the oldest mosques in India, has a traditional Kerala-style sloping roof.

topics.title: The growth of Sufism: khanqahs, silsilas and dargahs

learn.hook: Silsila means 'chain'. For Sufis, it was a spiritual chain linking each master and disciple all the way back to the Prophet Muhammad.
points: In the early centuries of Islam, a group of religious-minded people called Sufis turned to asceticism and mysticism in protest against the growing materialism of the Caliphate as a religious and political institution.

They were critical of dogmatic definitions and scholastic methods of interpreting the Qur'an and sunna (traditions of the Prophet) used by theologians. They emphasised seeking salvation through intense devotion and love for God, following the example of the Prophet, and interpreted the Qur'an on the basis of their personal experience.

By the eleventh century, Sufis organised communities around the hospice or khanqah (Persian), controlled by a teaching master known as a shaikh (Arabic), pir or murshid (Persian). He enrolled disciples (murids) and appointed a successor (khalifa).

Silsilas began to crystallise in the twelfth century. Silsila literally means a chain, signifying a continuous link between master and disciple, an unbroken spiritual genealogy going back to the Prophet. Some silsilas were named after a founder (Qadiri, after Shaikh Abd'ul Qadir Jilani), others after a place (Chishti, after the town of Chisht in Afghanistan).

When a shaikh died, his tomb-shrine, the dargah (Persian for 'court'), became a centre of devotion. Pilgrimage (ziyarat) was made especially on his death anniversary, the urs ('marriage'), signifying the union of his soul with God. Some mystics, such as the Qalandars, Madaris and Malangs, rejected khanqahs and defied the sharia; they were called be-shari'a, in contrast to the ba-shari'a Sufis who complied with it.

example.q: Why is the death anniversary of a Sufi saint called urs, 'marriage'?
steps: Sufis believed that in death the saint's soul united with God.
This union was seen as joyful, like a marriage.
So the anniversary is celebrated, not mourned.
example.answer: Because it marks the union of the saint's soul with God, which Sufis compared to a marriage.

learn.reallife: The urs of Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti at Ajmer Sharif, Rajasthan, draws lakhs of pilgrims of many faiths every year.

topics.title: The Chishtis: khanqah life and devotion at Ajmer

learn.hook: Emperor Akbar visited the dargah of Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti at Ajmer fourteen times, sometimes walking there to fulfil a vow!
points: Of the groups of Sufis who migrated to India in the late twelfth century, the Chishtis were the most influential, because they adapted successfully to the local environment and adopted several features of Indian devotional traditions.

Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya's hospice (fourteenth century) was at Ghiyaspur, on the banks of the Yamuna on the outskirts of Delhi. It had several small rooms and a big hall (jama'at khana) where inmates and visitors lived and prayed. The Shaikh lived in a small room on the roof and met visitors morning and evening.

An open kitchen (langar) was run on futuh (unasked-for charity). From morning till late night, people from all walks of life, including soldiers, slaves, singers, merchants, poets, travellers, rich and poor, Hindu jogis and qalandars, came seeking discipleship, amulets for healing and the Shaikh's intercession. Visitors included the poet Amir Khusrau and the historian Ziyauddin Barani.

Pilgrimage (ziyarat) to the tombs of Sufi saints was common. The most revered shrine is that of Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti, 'Gharib Nawaz' (comforter of the poor), at Ajmer. Muhammad bin Tughlaq was the first Sultan to visit it.

Akbar visited the Ajmer dargah fourteen times, sometimes two or three times a year, to seek blessings for conquests, the fulfilment of vows and the birth of sons. In 1643, Jahanara, daughter of Shah Jahan, wrote of her pilgrimage there, describing how she did not stretch her feet towards the tomb and prayed facing it.

example.q: Why did people of every background visit Nizamuddin Auliya's khanqah?
steps: The langar fed everyone, regardless of status.
People sought discipleship, healing amulets and the Shaikh's intercession.
The khanqah welcomed soldiers, slaves, merchants, poets, jogis and qalandars.
So it became a meeting place for all sections of society.
example.answer: Because it was open to all, offered food, spiritual guidance and blessings, and welcomed people of every background.

learn.reallife: The langar tradition of feeding everyone free of charge continues at Sufi dargahs like Nizamuddin in Delhi and at gurdwaras across India.

topics.title: Sama, languages and Sufis and the state

learn.hook: Every qawwali at the shrine of Nizamuddin Auliya begins with a qaul, a form introduced by Amir Khusrau over 700 years ago!
points: Music and dance, including mystical chants by qawwals, were part of Chishti devotion. The ritual of sama (audition, or musical gatherings) was integral to the Chishtis and showed their openness to local devotional traditions.

Amir Khusrau (1253–1325), the great poet, musician and disciple of Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya, gave a unique form to the Chishti sama by introducing the qaul (Arabic for 'saying'), a hymn sung at the opening or closing of qawwali. Qawwals at Nizamuddin's shrine still begin with the qaul.

The Chishtis conversed in Hindavi, the language of the people. Baba Farid composed verses in the local language, which were incorporated into the Guru Granth Sahib. Some Sufis composed long poems (masnavis) expressing divine love through human love, such as Malik Muhammad Jayasi's Padmavat, about Padmini and Ratansen, king of Chittor.

The Chishti tradition stressed austerity and distance from worldly power, but not total isolation. Sufis accepted unsolicited grants and donations; sultans set up charitable trusts (auqaf) and granted tax-free land (inam) to hospices. Chishtis preferred to use donations on immediate needs like food, clothes, living quarters and sama rather than accumulate wealth.

Kings sought the support of Sufis, whose piety gave legitimacy. Occasionally there was conflict between sultans and Sufi shaikhs, as both expected rituals like prostration and kissing of feet; Nizamuddin's disciples addressed him as sultan-ul-mashaikh (sultan among shaikhs).

example.q: Why did Sufis keep a distance from political power yet accept grants from rulers?
steps: Chishtis valued austerity and independence.
But they needed resources for the langar, lodging and sama.
They accepted unsolicited grants, not demands.
And used them for immediate needs rather than accumulating wealth.
example.answer: They accepted unsolicited support to serve visitors and rituals, while avoiding dependence and accumulation, keeping their spiritual independence.

learn.reallife: Qawwali at Delhi's Nizamuddin dargah on Thursday evenings is famous, and Amir Khusrau's songs like 'Chhap Tilak' are still sung in films and concerts.

learn.hook: 'The lotus which blooms without a flower, the fire raging in the ocean': Kabir loved upside-down sayings that turn everyday meaning on its head!
points: Kabir (c. fourteenth–fifteenth centuries) is one of the most remarkable poet-saints. His verses have been compiled in three distinct but overlapping traditions: the Kabir Bijak, preserved by the Kabirpanth in Varanasi and elsewhere in Uttar Pradesh; the Kabir Granthavali, associated with the Dadupanth in Rajasthan; and many compositions in the Adi Granth Sahib. All were compiled long after his death.

Kabir's poems are in several languages and dialects. Some are in sant bhasha, the language of the nirguna poets. Others, known as ulatbansi (upside-down sayings), invert everyday meanings, such as 'the lotus which blooms without flower' or 'the fire raging in the ocean', hinting at the difficulty of capturing the Ultimate Reality in words.

Kabir drew on many traditions to describe the Ultimate Reality: from Islam, terms like Allah, Khuda, Hazrat and Pir; from Vedantic traditions, terms like alakh (the unseen), nirakar (formless), Brahman and Atman; and from yogic traditions, terms like shabda (sound) and shunya (emptiness).
He rejected external worship in both Brahmanical Hinduism and Islam, criticising rituals, idol worship and the pre-eminence of the priestly classes.

Kabir's origins are debated. Vaishnava hagiographies suggest he was born a Hindu but raised by a poor Muslim weaver (julaha) family, and that he was initiated by a guru, perhaps Ramananda. But his verses use the words guru and satguru without naming a preceptor, and it is hard to show Ramananda and Kabir were contemporaries without assigning improbably long lives to them.

example.q: Why do historians hesitate to accept that Ramananda was Kabir's guru?
steps: Hagiographies make the claim.
Kabir's own verses mention 'guru' and 'satguru' but name no preceptor.
Making them contemporaries requires improbably long lives.
So the link is doubtful, though it shows how important Kabir's legacy was.
example.answer: Because Kabir's verses name no guru and the dates do not fit without improbably long lives, so the tradition cannot be accepted at face value.

learn.reallife: Kabir's dohas are part of Hindi school textbooks across India, and singers like Prahlad Singh Tipanya keep Kabir's songs alive in Madhya Pradesh's Malwa folk tradition.

topics.title: Baba Guru Nanak and the sacred word

learn.hook: Guru Nanak sang his hymns in ragas while his companion Mardana played the rabab. These shabads became the heart of a new community.
points: Baba Guru Nanak (1469–1539) was born into a Hindu merchant family in a village called Nankana Sahib near the river Ravi in the predominantly Muslim Punjab. He trained to be an accountant and studied Persian, but spent most of his time among Sufis and bhaktas and travelled widely.

He advocated a form of nirguna bhakti. He firmly repudiated the external practices of the religions around him: sacrifices, ritual baths, image worship, austerities and the scriptures of both Hindus and Muslims. For him, the Absolute or 'rab' had no gender or form.

He proposed a simple way to connect with the Divine: remembering and repeating the Divine Name, expressed in hymns called shabad in Punjabi. He sang them in various ragas while his attendant Mardana played the rabab. He organised his followers into a community with rules for congregational worship (sangat) and appointed his disciple Angad to succeed him as guru.

Guru Arjan compiled Baba Guru Nanak's hymns, along with those of his four successors and other poets like Baba Farid, Ravidas (Raidas) and Kabir, in the Adi Granth Sahib in 1604. Guru Gobind Singh later added the compositions of the ninth guru, Guru Tegh Bahadur, and the scripture came to be called the Guru Granth Sahib.

In 1699, Guru Gobind Singh laid the foundation of the Khalsa Panth (army of the pure) and defined its five symbols: uncut hair, a dagger, a pair of shorts, a comb and a steel bangle. Under him the community became consolidated as a socio-religious and military force.

example.q: How did Guru Nanak's message differ from ritual-based religion?
steps: He rejected sacrifices, ritual baths, image worship and austerities.
He taught that the Divine has no form or gender.
He proposed remembering and repeating the Divine Name through shabad.
He organised congregational worship (sangat).
example.answer: He replaced rituals with remembrance of the formless Divine through hymns and collective worship.

learn.reallife: Guru Nanak's birth anniversary, Gurpurab, is a national holiday in India; the Kartarpur Corridor opened in 2019 lets Indian pilgrims visit Gurdwara Darbar Sahib in Pakistan, where he spent his last years.

learn.hook: A Rajput princess who left the palace to sing for Krishna, guided, some say, by a leather-worker saint: Mirabai broke more than one rule!
points: Mirabai (c. fifteenth–sixteenth centuries) is perhaps the best-known woman poet in the bhakti tradition. Her biography has been reconstructed mainly from bhajans attributed to her, transmitted orally for centuries.
According to these, she was a Rajput princess from Merta in Marwar, married against her wishes to a prince of the Sisodia clan of Mewar, Rajasthan.

She defied her husband and did not submit to the traditional role of wife and mother. Instead she recognised Krishna, the avatar of Vishnu, as her lover. Her in-laws tried to poison her, but she escaped from the palace to live as a wandering singer, composing songs of intense devotion.

According to some traditions, her preceptor was Raidas, a leather worker, which would indicate her defiance of the norms of caste society. After leaving the palace she is said to have worn the white robes of a widow or the saffron robe of a renouncer.

Mirabai did not attract a sect or group of followers, but she has been a source of inspiration for centuries. Her songs are still sung by women and men, especially by those considered 'low caste' in Gujarat and Rajasthan.

example.q: Summarise the major teachings of Kabir, Guru Nanak and Mirabai.
steps: Kabir: formless Ultimate Reality; rejected rituals of Hinduism and Islam.
Guru Nanak: nirguna bhakti; remembering the Divine Name; sangat.
Mirabai: saguna devotion to Krishna; defied family and caste norms.
All three emphasised personal devotion over ritual.
example.answer: Kabir and Nanak taught devotion to a formless God and rejected rituals; Mirabai expressed loving devotion to Krishna and defied social norms.

learn.reallife: Mirabai's bhajans like 'Payoji maine Ram ratan dhan payo' are sung across India, and M.S. Subbulakshmi's 1945 film 'Meera' made her songs famous nationwide.

quiz.q: According to some traditions, Mirabai's preceptor was:
quiz.explain: Raidas, a leather worker, is said to be her guru.

quiz.q: Mirabai's biography has been reconstructed mainly from:
options: Bhajans attributed to her, transmitted orally
quiz.explain: Her songs, passed down orally, are the main source.

quiz.q: Which statement about Mirabai's legacy is correct?
options: She did not found a sect, but her songs are still sung, especially by those considered 'low caste' in Gujarat and Rajasthan
Her songs are sung only in Tamil Nadu
She was forgotten after her death
quiz.explain: Her influence lives on through her songs.

quiz.q: Mirabai's devotion is an example of:
quiz.explain: Devotion to Krishna, a deity with attributes, is saguna bhakti.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Mirabai's choice of Raidas as her guru, according to some traditions, was significant.
Reason (R): It showed her defiance of the norms of caste society, since Raidas was a leather worker.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A princess taking a leather worker as guru defied caste norms; R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Misses the social meaning of the choice.

learn.hook: A Persian poet sat with Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya and wrote down his conversations. That record, the Fawa'id-al-Fu'ad, is one of our best windows into Sufi life!
points: Historians use many sources to reconstruct religious traditions: sculpture and architecture, stories about religious preceptors, compositions attributed to women and men, and hagiographies written by followers.

Sufi traditions produced special kinds of texts. Malfuzat (literally 'uttered') are conversations of Sufi saints. An early example is the Fawa'id-al-Fu'ad, a collection of conversations of Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya, compiled by Amir Hasan Sijzi Dehlavi, a noted Persian poet.
Maktubat (literally 'writings') are letters written by Sufi masters to their disciples and associates, giving insight into their spiritual experiences and their lives.

Tazkiras (from Arabic, 'to mention, memorialise') are biographical accounts of saints. The first Sufi tazkira written in India was Mir Khwurd Kirmani's Siyar-ul-Auliya (fourteenth century), mainly about Chishti saints. A famous later one is Abdul Haqq Muhaddis Dehlavi's Akhbar-ul-Akhyar (1590).

Challenges: many traditions were transmitted orally and reworked over time, so there are many versions; compositions are in many regional languages; and hagiographies were written by followers who may not have been concerned with exact historical accuracy. Historians need to understand many languages and read sources critically.

example.q: A historian wants to study Nizamuddin Auliya's ideas. Which sources would she use and what caution would she take?
steps: Use the malfuzat, Fawa'id-al-Fu'ad, for his conversations.
Use tazkiras like Siyar-ul-Auliya for his life.
Use poems by disciples like Amir Khusrau.
Remember these were written by devotees, so read critically and compare.
example.answer: Malfuzat, tazkiras and disciples' poetry, read critically since they were written by admirers.

learn.reallife: Today, oral history projects in India record the songs of Baul singers in Bengal and Kabirpanthi singers in Malwa before these living traditions change further.

quiz.explain: Malfuzat literally means 'uttered'.

quiz.q: Who compiled the Fawa'id-al-Fu'ad?
quiz.explain: Amir Hasan Sijzi Dehlavi compiled it.

quiz.q: Maktubat literally means:
quiz.explain: Maktubat are letters, literally writings.

quiz.q: Which was the first Sufi tazkira written in India?
quiz.explain: Siyar-ul-Auliya (fourteenth century) was the first.

quiz.q: Akhbar-ul-Akhyar (1590) was written by:
quiz.explain: Abdul Haqq Muhaddis Dehlavi wrote it.

quiz.q: Which is a major challenge in reconstructing the history of bhakti and Sufi traditions?
options: There are no sources at all
Only one version of each poem exists
Oral transmission produced many versions in many regional languages
quiz.explain: Many versions and languages make reconstruction complex.

quiz.q: Why must historians read hagiographies critically?
options: They were written by followers who may not have been concerned with historical accuracy
quiz.explain: Devotional purposes shaped hagiographies.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): There are often many versions of a bhakti poem.
Reason (R): Many compositions were transmitted orally and reworked over time.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Oral transmission and reworking produced multiple versions; R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks variation came only from copying errors.
